title: Sita's question about the bow
hook: before Rama meets Agastya, Sita asks whether he should carry weapons at all: ahimsa and the protector's bow
carry: ahimsa, and a bow carried only to protect

segments.voice: Yesterday: sharanam: whoever takes refuge is protected. The sages showed Rama the bones, and he promised to stand between them and the rakshasas.

They're walking between hermitages, Rama ahead with his bow, Sita in the middle, Lakshmana behind. The path is narrow, the trees close, and nobody has spoken for a while. Then Sita, quietly, starts to talk. She's been thinking about that promise. She doesn't doubt Rama's goodness. She's worried about something else. You vowed to kill the rakshasas, and they haven't done anything to you. I'm afraid of what weapons do to the person who carries them.
screen: `SITA STARTS TO TALK.` → `THEY'VE DONE NOTHING TO YOU.` → `WHAT WEAPONS DO TO THEIR BEARER.`

segments.voice: She lays out her worry carefully. Three faults come from desire, she says: speaking falsely, wanting someone else's wife, and violence without enmity, harming those who haven't harmed you. You've never done the first two. The third worries me. Then she tells a story. Once Indra, uneasy at an ascetic's power, came disguised as a warrior and left a sword with him for safekeeping. The ascetic carried it everywhere, to gather fruit, to bathe, to pray, and slowly, without noticing, he grew rough, then cruel, and lost his practice. Fire, she says, is kindled by being near fuel. I only say this out of love. Rama's answer is just as tender. You say this because you care for me. But a warrior carries a bow so that no one in distress cries out unheard. The sages came to me for refuge, and I gave my word. Hindus have a name for what Sita is guarding: ahimsa, not harming. It comes first in yoga's list of restraints, and it's a big reason many Hindus eat vegetarian. And Rama names the other half: dharma can ask you to protect. That's why gods on a Hindu altar hold weapons in some hands and bless with another. Many teachers read those weapons as guarding dharma, never harming the innocent. The text lets both speak. Then ten years pass in the hermitages of Dandaka, and the road leads to Agastya.
screen: `THREE FAULTS FROM DESIRE.` · `THE ASCETIC AND THE SWORD.` · `NO ONE CRIES OUT UNHEARD.` · `AHIMSA, AND THE PROTECTOR'S BOW.` · then, large: `TWO GOOD PEOPLE, BOTH HEARD.`

segments.voice: Many Hindus close a prayer with Om shanti, shanti, shanti: peace, three times. Let your hands rest empty in your lap, as if you'd set down the ascetic's sword. If you pray, say it slowly, once for yourself, once for the people near you, once for the world. If you don't, breathe out peace three times, for the same three.
Agastya's weapons. Before the sage gives Rama weapons, Sita asks whether carrying them will change him, and Rama answers with his promise.
Your line: ahimsa, and a bow carried only to protect. Sita said it out of love, and Rama heard it that way. Day five hundred fifty-seven, done.

howItsDone: Reciters give Sita's question about weapons in the Aranya Kanda its full length, and Hindu teachers who discuss it note that the text lets both her concern and Rama's answer stand.
